The storm came in sideways, the way they always did at Thornfield Point — not from the horizon but from some angry fold in the sky that seemed to open directly above the lighthouse. Elias Mercer stood at the gallery rail, rain lashing his oilskin, and watched the sea turn itself inside out.

Three years. Three years since Catherine's funeral, since he'd traded their cottage in Harrowby for this granite tower at the edge of the world. The townspeople called it exile. Elias called it peace. He had always been a man who trusted what he could see, measure, and predict — tides, weather patterns, the exact second the light needed winding. The world was mechanical. It followed rules.

The light behind him swept its arc — fifteen seconds on, five seconds dark — painting the churning water in rhythmic slashes of white. He'd memorized the timing the way other men memorized prayers. It was the only conversation he needed.

When the storm finally spent itself near dawn on October 12th, Elias climbed down to the rocks to check for damage. The tide had thrown its usual debris against the base of the tower: kelp, driftwood, a shattered lobster pot. But wedged in the crevice between two boulders, something caught his eye. A glass bottle, intact, sealed with red wax.

Inside was a folded slip of paper. The handwriting was cramped but precise: "October 14th — the fishing trawler Mary Ellen will capsize at the harbor mouth. Two aboard. Both survive but only because someone on the north jetty throws a line."

Elias read it twice, then laughed — a dry, unused sound. Predictions. Fortune-telling. The kind of nonsense Catherine had loved and he had gently mocked. Some bored teenager's idea of a game, nothing more. He pocketed the note and forgot about it.

Two days later, on October 14th, he was buying supplies at the harbor shop when shouting broke out on the waterfront. He reached the north jetty in time to see the Mary Ellen roll in a rogue swell, her hull lifting clear of the water before slamming back down inverted. Two figures thrashed in the foam.

Elias stood frozen, the slip of paper burning in his coat pocket like a coal. This was not possible. The world did not work this way. Tides followed the moon, storms followed pressure systems, boats capsized from mechanical failure — not because a note in a bottle said they would. But the words were exact. The date, the boat's name, the location. Exact.

Before he could think, a dockworker beside him threw a coiled rope. Both men were pulled to safety, coughing seawater onto the stone jetty.

That night, back in the lighthouse, Elias smoothed the slip of paper on his desk and read it a third time. His hands were shaking. The lamp oil filled the room with its familiar amber smell, and below the gallery the waves kept their ancient, indifferent rhythm against the rocks.

He walked to the rail and stared at the dark waterline. Somewhere out there, between the current and the continental shelf, there had to be more bottles. And he was going to find every single one.
